# Heterogeneous Compute Placement\chaptersubtitle{Silicon Interconnects, Memory Bus QoS, and Thermal Envelopes}

![**Systems Organ Focus:** Whole-System Heterogeneous Silicon Placement across Cloud, Host MPU, Neural Accelerator NPU, and Real-Time MCU. Physical AI partitions cognitive stages across silicon fabrics based on execution cadence, memory bandwidth, thermal dissipation, and safety isolation boundaries.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch10 width=100% fig-pos="H"}

*Why does an autonomous robot that runs flawlessly on the test bench suffer violent latency spikes when deployed inside a sealed chassis?*

In cloud software architecture, computation is treated as an abstract, fungible commodity: microservices are deployed into elastic clusters where physical silicon placement is hidden behind virtualization layers. In Physical AI, silicon topology is a non-negotiable physical boundary. Moving bits across off-chip memory buses consumes orders of magnitude more energy than arithmetic, shared memory crossbars choke when camera DMA bursts contend with neural weight streaming, and unmanaged thermal dissipation triggers hardware downclocking that blows past real-time stopping deadlines. Designing an embodied system requires deliberate workload placement—mapping cognitive stages across cloud servers, Linux host processors, neural accelerators, and real-time microcontrollers based on cadence, memory bandwidth, and physical trust boundaries.

{{< pagebreak >}}

After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Map Cognitive Organs to Silicon Fabrics:** Partition the five sensory-motor organs across Cloud, Host Processor (MPU), Neural Accelerator (NPU), and Real-Time Microcontroller (MCU) fabrics based on cadence ($0.001\text{ Hz} \to 1000\text{ Hz}$), memory bandwidth, and trust boundaries.
2. **Mitigate Interconnect Contention:** Architect hardware AXI Quality-of-Service (QoS) bus arbitration schemes that guarantee microsecond preemption for real-time safety packets over high-bandwidth video DMA bursts.
3. **Implement Deterministic Shared-Memory IPC:** Construct lock-free, zero-allocation circular ring buffers in tightly coupled SRAM using 64-bit atomic sequence counters and explicit cache maintenance operations.
4. **Quantify the Energy Cost of Data Movement:** Balance arithmetic intensity ($\text{FLOPs/Byte}$) against LPDDR5 DRAM access energy ($150\text{ pJ/access}$) using on-chip SRAM model weight tiling.
5. **Model Dynamic Thermal Dissipation & DVFS:** Derive the junction heating differential equation ($T_j(t)$) and design proactive cadence scaling to prevent thermal downclocking cliffs ($>85^\circ\text{C}$).
6. **Evaluate Re-Placement Ripple Effects:** Quantify how migrating neural models between cloud and edge silicon alters network round-trip jitter, battery endurance, and physical stopping clearance envelopes ($d_{\text{stop}}$).
7. **Dissect Wireless Network Latency Collisions:** Analyze the Insulated Cold-Vault Collision autopsy where a $1,420\text{ ms}$ 5G RF blackout caused a 1.2-ton pallet mover to smash into a structural building pillar at $1.8\text{ m/s}$.
8. **Freeze the Workload Placement Ledger:** Author the formal engineering specification establishing whole-system hardware allocations, interconnect QoS priorities, and thermal derating regimes.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** Physical AI computation is fundamentally non-fungible; mapping multi-rate cognitive organs across heterogeneous silicon fabrics requires co-designing arithmetic intensity, memory crossbar QoS arbitration, lock-free SRAM mailboxes, and thermal dissipation envelopes to prevent dynamic throttling from breaching real-time control deadlines.

## The Non-Fungibility of Compute in Physical Systems

In modern enterprise software engineering, computation is abstracted behind virtualized infrastructure. Developers write containerized services, dispatch tasks to elastic serverless runtimes, and interact with cloud APIs under the assumption that processing power is fungible. If a database query encounters transient congestion or a network packet drops, execution threads block, retry logic absorbs delays, and garbage collectors sweep memory without physical consequence.

In Physical AI Systems, compute is fundamentally **non-fungible** (@fig-heterogeneous-placement). The moment software interacts with physical mass, inertia, and electrical current, the physical location of silicon determines whether the machine survives:

1. **The Physicality of Latency:** Running a 70-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model in a remote cloud datacenter provides immense semantic capacity. However, routing sensor video over a cellular 5G network introduces stochastic Round-Trip Time (RTT) variance ($50\text{--}1500\text{ ms}$) and unannounced RF signal dropouts. If a 1.2-ton mobile machine traveling at $v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$ loses wireless connectivity for one second, the vehicle coasts unguided for two meters ($d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t = 2.0\text{ m}$), turning a wireless packet drop into an unavoidable collision.
2. **The Physics of Memory Energy:** Moving bits across printed circuit board traces consumes orders of magnitude more electrical energy than performing arithmetic operations on those bits. In modern $7\text{ nm}$ silicon, executing an 8-bit integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation consumes approximately $0.2\text{ pJ}$, whereas fetching the operand bytes from off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM consumes $150\text{ pJ}$—a $750\times$ energy disparity.
3. **The Thermodynamic Real-Time Cliff:** Compute chips generate thermal energy ($P = I^2 R + C_{\text{gate}} V^2 f$). In a sealed robotic chassis lacking heavy active cooling, sustained neural inference drives silicon junction temperatures past critical thresholds ($T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$). Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) circuits automatically cut clock frequencies by up to $60\%$, doubling inference latency and causing the robot to miss its hard real-time stopping deadlines.

![**The Four-Tier Heterogeneous Compute Topology in Physical AI.** System 2 semantic deliberation maps to Tier 3 Linux MPUs or Tier 4 Cloud clusters; System 1.5 trajectory chunking maps to Tier 2 NPUs; System 1 reflex enforcers map to Tier 1 bare-metal MCUs with direct physical routing to motor inverters.](figures/fig09_heterogeneous_placement.svg){#fig-heterogeneous-placement width=100%}

To satisfy these physical constraints, Physical AI partitions cognitive workloads across a **Four-Tier Heterogeneous Silicon Hierarchy** (@tbl-compute-tiers):

| Compute Fabric Tier | Hardware Substrate | Primary Architectural Role & Cognitive Organ | Typical Execution Cadence | Memory Architecture | Physical Trust Level |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 4: Cloud / Fleet** | Multi-GPU Datacenter Cluster | Fleet learning, large foundational pre-training, global routing *(Deliberation Archive)* | $0.001\text{--}0.1\text{ Hz}$ | Terabytes HBM3 / NVMe Storage | **Untrusted:** Non-deterministic WAN latency |
| **Tier 3: Host Processor (MPU)** | 64-bit Multi-Core ARM Cortex-A | Semantic reasoning (VLMs), dynamic frame trees (`tf2`) *(Organ 3: Deliberation & Memory)* | $0.5\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$ | 4–16 GB LPDDR5 Unified Memory (UMA) | **Untrusted:** Non-real-time OS jitter ($P_{99} > 100\text{ ms}$) |
| **Tier 2: Neural Accelerator (NPU)** | Systolic Array / Edge Tensor Cores | Spatial affordances (DINOv2), Action Chunking (ACT, Diffusion) *(Organ 2: Policy & Action)* | $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ | On-Chip SRAM Tiling + DRAM DMA | **Untrusted Proposal Service:** High-throughput tensor compute |

## Silicon Interconnects and Memory Bus Contention: AXI Crossbars and QoS Arbitration

In modern embedded Systems-on-Chip (SoCs)—such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, Qualcomm Robotics RB5, or Apple M-series silicon—heterogeneous compute engines (CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP, and DMA engines) share a single pool of physical LPDDR5 DRAM through a **Unified Memory Architecture (UMA)** (@fig-uma-contention).

![**UMA Memory Bus Contention and AXI QoS Priority Arbitration.** High-bandwidth camera sensor DMA writes ($>1.5\text{ GB/s}$) and NPU model weight fetches ($20\text{ GB/s}$) contend for shared memory crossbars. Without hardware AXI QoS arbitration, unthrottled DMA bursts starve real-time microcontroller reads, causing $1000\text{ Hz}$ safety loops to miss timing deadlines.](figures/fig09_uma_bus_contention.svg){#fig-uma-contention width=100%}

While UMA eliminates the physical PCIe copying overhead found in desktop computers, it introduces a severe micro-architectural vulnerability: **Memory Crossbar Contention**. In an unmanaged UMA SoC, multiple bus masters issue memory transactions simultaneously across shared AXI interconnect crossbars:

1. High-resolution multi-camera image sensors write raw uncompressed Bayer frames directly to DRAM via MIPI CSI-2 DMA engines ($1.5\text{--}3.0\text{ GB/s}$ sustained).
2. The Neural Processing Unit streams billions of quantized model weights from DRAM into local tensor registers during forward passes ($15\text{--}30\text{ GB/s}$ burst bandwidth).
3. The Real-Time Microcontroller reads joint encoder buffers and writes candidate trajectory waypoints.

When an unthrottled camera DMA burst saturates the memory crossbar, DRAM access latency for CPU and NPU cores spikes by $300\text{--}800\%$. A deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ microcontroller thread attempting to read a trajectory waypoint from shared memory is stalled, causing the real-time loop to miss its $1.0\text{ ms}$ control deadline.

To prevent memory starvation, Physical AI architectures configure hardware **AXI Quality-of-Service (QoS)** arbitration registers (the 4-bit `ARQOS` read and `AWQOS` write priority signals, ranging from 0 to 15) at the silicon interconnect fabric:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{AXI QoS Invariant:} \quad &\text{QoS}(\text{MCU Real-Time Reads}) \\
&> \text{QoS}(\text{NPU Weight Fetches}) \\
&> \text{QoS}(\text{Camera DMA Writes})
\end{aligned}$$

1. **Real-Time MCU Mailbox Reads (`QoS = 15`):** Absolute highest interconnect priority. When the MCU reads shared trajectory waypoints across the system crossbar, arbiters immediately grant next-cycle bus access ahead of queued DMA bursts, guaranteeing service within $<50\text{ ns}$.
2. **NPU Tensor Weight Fetches (`QoS = 10`):** High priority, guaranteeing sustained memory throughput to meet $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ action chunking deadlines.
3. **Camera Sensor DMA Writes (`QoS = 4`):** Background priority. Camera DMA streams are buffered in dedicated on-chip FIFO buffers and paced onto the crossbar only during memory bus idle cycles, eliminating latency tail blowouts.


## Deterministic Inter-Processor Communication: Zero-Copy Shared SRAM Mailboxes and Lock-Free Ring Buffers

To pass high-rate trajectory chunks ($50\text{ Hz}$) and low-latency safety telemetry ($1000\text{ Hz}$) between the Linux host processor (MPU) and the bare-metal microcontroller (MCU) without thread blocking, Physical AI rejects traditional operating system inter-process communication primitives. Standard POSIX mutexes, Unix domain sockets, and named pipes rely on Linux kernel scheduler intervention. When a real-time thread encounters a contested mutex or waits on a pipe under standard kernel scheduling, the resulting context switch introduces up to $50\text{ ms}$ of scheduling jitter—a delay fifty times longer than the entire $1.0\text{ ms}$ control budget of a $1000\text{ Hz}$ reflex loop.

To achieve deterministic sub-microsecond transfers, inter-processor communication relies on zero-copy, lock-free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) ring buffers mapped into physical, internal static SRAM (Tightly Coupled Memory or TCM). Each slot in the circular mailbox is aligned to a 64-byte hardware cache line boundary (`alignas(64)`) to eliminate false sharing between cores. False sharing occurs when logically distinct variables share a single physical cache line: whenever one core updates its variable, the hardware cache coherency protocol invalidates the entire 64-byte line across all other cores, triggering expensive interconnect snooping cycles and stalling execution pipelines.

```c
// LOCK-FREE INTER-PROCESSOR COMMUNICATION BUFFER (Shared Static SRAM)
#define SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS 3
#define CACHE_LINE_SIZE   64
#define MAILBOX_MAGIC     0x50485953  // "PHYS"

typedef struct {
    uint32_t magic_header;
    uint32_t payload_crc32;
    uint64_t sequence_id;
    trajectory_chunk_t trajectory;
} alignas(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) mailbox_slot_t;

typedef struct {
    // Producer sequence cache line (written by Linux MPU, polled by MCU)
    alignas(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) volatile uint64_t head_sequence;
    
    // Consumer sequence cache line (written by MCU, polled by Linux MPU)
    alignas(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) volatile uint64_t tail_sequence;
    
    // Triple-buffered payload arena (zero dynamic memory allocation)
    mailbox_slot_t slots[SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS];
} alignas(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) lockless_sram_mailbox_t;
```

The triple-buffered mailbox operates under strict memory ordering and cache maintenance invariants across heterogeneous hardware domains:

First, monotonic 64-bit sequence counters coordinate data visibility without locks. The producer writes trajectory data into slot $k = \text{head\_sequence} \pmod 3$, computes the payload CRC32, and publishes the update by incrementing `head_sequence` using a 64-bit atomic store with release memory semantics (`__atomic_store_n(&head, seq, __ATOMIC_RELEASE)`). The consumer samples `head_sequence` using an acquire memory load (`__atomic_load_n(&head, __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE)`). The release-acquire barrier pair guarantees that all payload writes are committed to physical memory before the updated sequence counter becomes visible to the consumer.

Second, when bridging non-coherent memory domains—such as an ARM Cortex-A application processor operating through cached L1/L2 hierarchies and an ARM Cortex-M7 executing out of tightly coupled memory—software must explicitly execute cache maintenance routines:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Producer Write Sequence:} \quad &\text{write\_payload}(\text{slot}_k) \\
&\implies \text{clean\_dcache\_range}(\&\text{slot}_k, \text{sizeof}) \\
&\implies \text{atomic\_store}(\text{head})
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Consumer Read Sequence:} \quad &\text{atomic\_load}(\text{head}) \\
&\implies \text{invalidate\_dcache\_range}(\&\text{slot}_k, \text{sizeof}) \\
&\implies \text{read\_payload}(\text{slot}_k)
\end{aligned}$$

Cleaning the data cache forces dirty cache lines out to physical SRAM, while invalidating the data cache discards stale cache entries so the consumer reads newly written payload bytes directly from SRAM rather than cached remnants.

Third, the interface enforces latest-frame sampling semantics. If the neural policy publishes trajectory chunks faster than the reflex controller consumes them, the microcontroller does not queue stale messages. Instead, it computes the latest published index $k = \text{head\_sequence} \pmod 3$ and drops intermediate frames. In physical control systems, queueing outdated trajectory plans creates dangerous phase lag; consuming only the freshest available plan guarantees zero latency accumulation.


## Arithmetic Intensity vs. Memory Bandwidth: The Physics of Data Movement

In embodied robotic design, total power consumption is tightly constrained by onboard battery capacity and chassis thermal dissipation limits. Because electrical energy drawn from the battery is dissipated as heat, algorithms must be co-designed for **Arithmetic Intensity** ($I_{\text{arith}}$), defined as the ratio of computational floating-point operations performed to the total volume of memory traffic transferred across the memory bus [@hennessy2019computer]:

$$I_{\text{arith}} = \frac{\text{Total Computational Operations (FLOPs)}}{\text{Total Memory Bus Traffic (Bytes)}} \quad \left[ \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Byte}} \right]$$

The Williams and Hennessy Roofline Model establishes the upper bound on attainable computational performance for a given silicon architecture:

$$\text{Attainable Performance (FLOPs/s)} = \min\left( \text{Peak Compute Throughput}, \; I_{\text{arith}} \times \text{Peak Memory Bandwidth} \right)$$

The intersection between the memory-bandwidth diagonal and the peak-compute ceiling defines the silicon architecture's ridge point ($I_{\text{ridge}} = \text{Peak Compute} / \text{Peak Bandwidth}$). When an algorithm's arithmetic intensity falls below this ridge point, execution is strictly memory-bound: computational throughput is constrained not by arithmetic ALU capacity, but by the rate at which data bytes can be fetched from external DRAM.

Standard autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models suffer severely from this constraint during single-token generation. For a linear projection layer with weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$, computing a single output token vector $y = W x$ requires $2 d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}}$ floating-point operations (one multiply and one accumulate per parameter). In 16-bit precision (FP16 or BF16), loading the matrix from external DRAM requires fetching $2 d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}}$ bytes. The resulting arithmetic intensity is precisely unity:

$$I_{\text{arith, autoregressive}} = \frac{2 d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}} \text{ FLOPs}}{2 d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}} \text{ Bytes}} = 1.0 \quad \left[ \frac{\text{FLOP}}{\text{Byte}} \right]$$

On an edge accelerator capable of $100\text{ TFLOP/s}$ with an LPDDR5 memory bandwidth of $68\text{ GB/s}$, the ridge point is $100{,}000 / 68 \approx 1{,}470\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$. At an arithmetic intensity of $1.0\text{ FLOP/Byte}$, the attainable performance is capped at just $68\text{ GFLOP/s}$—less than $0.1\%$ of the accelerator's peak compute capacity. Tensor ALUs remain idle over $99\%$ of the time waiting for DRAM wordlines to recharge, while high-frequency memory bus I/O drivers burn battery power and generate waste heat.

To break through the memory wall, Physical AI systems adopt three silicon placement and architectural optimizations:

First, small temporal trajectory decoders—such as 1D convolutional U-Nets for Diffusion Policy or Action Chunking Transformers—are quantized to INT8 or FP8 precision. Quantization compresses the full model footprint to under $8\text{ MB}$, allowing all layer weights to reside permanently inside the neural processing unit's on-chip static SRAM (TCM or tightly coupled cache).

Second, by retaining both model weights and intermediate feature maps entirely in on-chip SRAM across all diffusion denoising iterations, off-chip DRAM round-trip traffic is eliminated during trajectory generation. Model weights are loaded once and reused across all temporal action steps in the chunk ($H = 16\text{--}32$), driving arithmetic intensity above $I_{\text{arith}} > 150\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$.

Third, avoiding off-chip DRAM access produces massive thermodynamic and energy savings. In modern $7\text{ nm}$ silicon, fetching an operand from external LPDDR5 DRAM requires approximately $150\text{ pJ}$, whereas reading from on-chip SRAM requires only $1.5\text{ pJ}$—a $98.5\%$ reduction in data movement energy. Operating out of on-chip SRAM allows the neural accelerator to sustain continuous $50\text{ Hz}$ trajectory generation while consuming less than $15\text{ Watts}$ of electrical power.


## Thermal Design Power (TDP) and Dynamic Throttling (DVFS): The Thermal Envelope

All electrical energy consumed by silicon computing substrates is ultimately converted into thermal heat via Joule heating ($P = I^2 R$). In an embodied robot, compute silicon is frequently housed inside a sealed, IP67-rated water-resistant chassis lacking heavy active cooling fans (@fig-thermal-derating).

![**Thermodynamic Junction Heating and the DVFS Downclocking Cliff.** Sustained high-load neural inference dissipates thermal heat. When junction temperature breaches $T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$, hardware DVFS circuits downclock the accelerator by up to $60\%$, doubling inference latency and causing the robot to miss its real-time stopping deadlines. Proactive cadence scaling manages thermal equilibrium.](figures/fig09_thermal_derating_ripple.svg){#fig-thermal-derating width=100%}

The thermodynamic heat dissipation of the compute die is modeled by the first-order differential equation:

$$C_{\text{die}} \frac{d T_j(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{dynamic}}(t) + P_{\text{PHY}}(t) + P_{\text{leakage}}(T_j) - \frac{T_j(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}}{R_\theta}$$

where $T_j$ is the silicon junction temperature, $C_{\text{die}}$ is the thermal capacitance of the silicon package ($\text{J}/^\circ\text{C}$), $R_\theta$ is the lumped thermal resistance through the conduction-cooled chassis to ambient air ($^\circ\text{C}/\text{W}$), $P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha C_{\text{gate}} V^2 f$ is the active switching power (with activity factor $\alpha$, gate capacitance $C_{\text{gate}}$, supply voltage $V$, and clock frequency $f$), $P_{\text{PHY}}$ is memory I/O driver power, and $P_{\text{leakage}} \propto T_j^2$ is temperature-dependent static leakage current. Because leakage escalates quadratically with temperature, uncooled silicon risks a positive feedback loop: higher temperatures increase leakage power, which further drives up junction heat.

When sustained neural inference drives the junction temperature past the silicon safety knee ($T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$), on-chip thermal supervisory circuits trigger **Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS)**. To prevent silicon destruction, the hardware controller downclocks the accelerator:

$$f_{\text{clock}} \leftarrow 0.40 \times f_{\text{nominal}}$$

This sudden $60\%$ frequency collapse doubles trajectory inference latency ($T_{\text{infer}}: 25\text{ ms} \to 60\text{ ms}$), causing System 1.5 to miss its $50\text{ ms}$ action chunk deadline. Actuators are starved of fresh waypoints, intent leases expire, and the robot trips a hard emergency stop.

To eliminate thermal cliff collapses, Physical AI deploys **Proactive Thermal Cadence Scaling**. The firmware monitors on-die thermal diodes: when temperature reaches the warning knee ($T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C}$), the policy engine doubles the action chunk horizon ($H=16 \to 32$) and lowers inference invocation cadence from $50\text{ Hz}$ to $20\text{ Hz}$. Because a 32-step chunk executed at $50\text{ Hz}$ by the MCU provides $640\text{ ms}$ of valid trajectory lookahead, running the NPU once every $50\text{ ms}$ ($20\text{ Hz}$) maintains uninterrupted action streaming while cutting accelerator duty cycle and dynamic power by $60\%$, stabilizing junction heat safely below the $85^\circ\text{C}$ DVFS downclocking cliff.


## Re-Placement Ripple Effects: Evaluating Latency, Power, and Safety Migration

When designing a Physical AI system, architects frequently consider re-partitioning algorithms across compute fabrics (e.g., migrating a Vision-Language Model from an offboard cloud cluster to an onboard edge NPU, or shifting state estimation from an MCU to a Linux thread). 

Every re-placement decision triggers a multi-dimensional ripple effect across latency, power, thermal headroom, and safety (@tbl-placement-tradeoffs):

| Architectural Re-Placement Choice | Primary Advantage | Silicon Latency Impact | Thermal & Power Impact | Safety & Robustness Consequence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Offload System 2 VLA to Cloud / 5G** | Unlocks massive 70B parameter models; saves onboard battery | Adds $50\text{--}1500\text{ ms}$ WAN jitter; subject to RF drops | Reduces onboard compute power by $\sim 30\text{ W}$ | **Vulnerable:** Must enforce hard local MCU fallback leases |
| **Quantize VLA to 3B on Edge NPU** | Fully autonomous offline operation; zero RF network dependence | Deterministic $350\text{ ms}$ local inference latency | Increases onboard TDP by $25\text{ W}$; raises $T_j$ | **Robust:** Immune to wireless dropouts and jamming |
| **Move State Estimation from MCU to Linux MPU** | Access to rich ROS2 / Python sensor fusion libraries | Injects $5\text{--}50\text{ ms}$ OS scheduling jitter | Negligible power delta ($<1\text{ W}$) | **Dangerous:** OS page faults freeze state belief during motion |
| **Move Reflex CBF-QP from Linux to Bare-Metal MCU** | Deterministic sub-millisecond execution ($\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$) | Reduces safety response latency from $50\text{ ms} \to 1.0\text{ ms}$ | Negligible power footprint ($<0.5\text{ W}$) | **Provably Safe:** Hardware-isolated from OS stalls and crashes |

: Architectural Re-Placement Ripple Effects. Trade-offs across computational capability, latency determinism, thermal dissipation, and physical safety. {#tbl-placement-tradeoffs}

The cardinal rule of Physical AI placement dictates: **Never migrate time-critical safety authority across an asynchronous or non-deterministic boundary**. Semantic deliberation may be offloaded to cloud servers if protected by local intent leases, but real-time state estimation and reflex barrier enforcement must remain permanently anchored to local, bare-metal silicon.


## Systems Failure Anatomy: The Insulated Cold-Vault Collision & 5G Packet Blackout

The destructive physical reality of offloading time-critical policy execution across a non-deterministic wireless network is documented in the forensic autopsy of an autonomous heavy transport AGV.

::: {.callout-autopsy title="The Insulated Cold-Vault Collision"}
**Platform:** 1.2-ton Autonomous Heavy Pallet Mover ($m = 1{,}200\text{ kg}$, $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$).  
**Failure Mechanism:** To reduce onboard compute costs and thermal dissipation, the high-level VLA policy was offloaded to an edge 5G server; entering a cold-storage vault created an RF multipath and shadow blackout of $1,420\text{ ms}$.  
**Root Cause:** Drive torque commands remained latched at $240\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ during the wireless dropout without local fallback trajectory caches or an independent MCU stopping supervisor.  
**Physical Consequence:** The vehicle coasted unguided for $2.556\text{ m}$ ($+1.356\text{ m}$ past physical obstacle clearance), smashing into a structural steel pillar at $1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($E_k = 1{,}944\text{ J}$), shearing the front steering kingpin, rupturing hydraulic lines, and crushing lithium battery modules ($42{,}000\text{ USD}$ overhaul).  
:::

![The Autonomous Heavy Pallet Mover Platform. Offloading policy execution to a 5G edge server caused a fatal crash when entering a cold-storage vault that blocked RF signals for $1,420\text{ ms}$.](figures/fig09_agv_mover_cropped.jpg){#fig-agv-mover width=100%}

In this industrial incident, a 1.2-ton automated guided vehicle (AGV) was transporting heavy palletized goods across a distribution warehouse at an operational velocity of $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($6.48\text{ km/h}$) (@fig-agv-mover). To minimize onboard thermal dissipation, bill-of-materials cost, and battery consumption, systems architects offloaded the multi-camera vision-language-action (VLA) policy to an offboard edge computing server over a private 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) network.

At timestamp $T + 84.210\text{ s}$, the AGV crossed the doorway threshold into an industrial cold-storage refrigeration vault. The vault walls were constructed of double-sided steel-clad polyurethane insulation panels, forming a continuous Faraday cage. The RF signal-to-noise ratio collapsed immediately from $+24\text{ dB}$ to $0\text{ dB}$, and the 5G connection entered an unannounced $1,420\text{ ms}$ packet blackout.

Onboard the vehicle, the host processor maintained no local trajectory cache. The motor inverter controller was configured with a naive Zero-Order Hold that held the last received torque setpoint ($\tau_{\text{motor}} = 240\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) until a new command packet arrived. Lacking an autonomous bare-metal microcontroller evaluating dynamic stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}}$) or enforcing hardware heartbeat watchdog timeouts, the 1.2-ton machine coasted forward at full operational velocity:

$$d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{blackout}} = 1.8\text{ m/s} \times 1.420\text{ s} = 2.556\text{ m}$$

At the entrance of the vault, a structural steel building column was located at a physical clearance of $d_{\text{clearance}} = 1.20\text{ m}$. Because the vehicle traveled $2.556\text{ m}$ without initiating deceleration, it completely exhausted the available clearance buffer and overshot the impact point by:

$$\Delta d = d_{\text{coast}} - d_{\text{clearance}} = 2.556\text{ m} - 1.200\text{ m} = +1.356\text{ m}$$

The vehicle struck the solid steel column at full operational velocity ($v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$). With a total vehicle mass of $m = 1{,}200\text{ kg}$, the linear momentum carried into the collision was:

$$p = m v = 1{,}200\text{ kg} \times 1.8\text{ m/s} = 2{,}160\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s} = 2.16 \times 10^3\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$$

The kinetic energy dissipated during impact was:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1{,}200\text{ kg} \times (1.8\text{ m/s})^2 = 1{,}944\text{ Joules}$$

The structural deceleration shock sheared the $45\text{ mm}$ alloy-steel front steering kingpin, ruptured the $210\text{ bar}$ high-pressure hydraulic steering lines, and crushed the forward $48\text{ V}$ lithium iron phosphate ($\text{LiFePO}_4$) battery modules ($42{,}000\text{ USD}$ overhaul cost). The flight-recorder telemetry ledger is detailed in @tbl-telemetry-ch10.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls in Heterogeneous Compute Placement

Deploying neural policies onto embodied hardware requires dismantling digital software abstractions that treat computation as fungible, memory transfers as free, and wireless connectivity as deterministic.

#### Fallacy: High-Speed Wireless Networks Provide Determinism for Direct Control {.unnumbered}
Assuming that because 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) and Wi-Fi 7 offer nominal latencies of $1\text{--}5\text{ ms}$ and multi-gigabit throughput, high-level policies running on edge servers can directly stream real-time motor torque setpoints or close actuator loops over the air without onboard local safety supervision. In reality, RF propagation in industrial environments is fundamentally stochastic, subject to multipath fading, destructive interference nulls, shadow fading from moving metal equipment or steel-clad walls, and base station handoff stalls. While median round-trip time may be $3\text{ ms}$, tail latency ($P_{99.999}$) exhibits severe blowouts exceeding $1{,}000\text{--}2{,}000\text{ ms}$. In physical systems, unmonitored latency translates directly into unguided kinetic displacement ($d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{blackout}}$). For a 1.2-ton machine traveling at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$, a $1.42\text{ s}$ network drop results in $2.556\text{ m}$ of unguided travel—instantly exhausting local clearance envelopes ($1.20\text{ m}$) and causing catastrophic mechanical impact ($E_k = 1{,}944\text{ J}$). Closed-loop actuator authority requires provable, deterministic execution on local, physically connected bare-metal microcontrollers.

#### Fallacy: Shared Unified Memory (UMA) Eliminates All Data Movement Overhead {.unnumbered}
Believing that because modern embedded SoCs integrate CPU, GPU, and NPU into a Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) sharing a single physical LPDDR5 DRAM pool, zero-copy pointer passing eliminates all data movement latency, interconnect contention, and energy overhead. While UMA eliminates explicit PCIe bus copies, all compute engines must share the *same* physical DRAM memory controller and internal AXI crossbars. When high-bandwidth sensor DMAs ($2.5\text{ GB/s}$) and neural weight fetches ($20\text{ GB/s}$) saturate the crossbar, DRAM access latency for CPU and MCU threads spikes by $300\text{--}800\%$. Furthermore, accessing off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM consumes $\approx 150\text{ pJ/access}$ vs $<2\text{ pJ/access}$ for on-chip static SRAM ($75\times$ energy disparity), demonstrating that UMA is a shared contention domain requiring strict hardware AXI QoS arbitration and on-chip SRAM weight tiling.

#### Pitfall: DVFS Downclocking Induced by Model Memory Bandwidth Thrashing {.unnumbered}
Deploying neural network policies with low arithmetic intensity ($I_{\text{arith}} \approx 1\text{--}2\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$) that continuously stream multi-gigabyte weight tensors across off-chip DRAM buses in passively cooled or IP67-sealed robotic enclosures. In low-arithmetic-intensity models, memory PHY I/O pads and DRAM controllers dissipate substantial Joulean power alongside active silicon switching. When sustained memory thrashing drives junction temperature past the hardware threshold ($T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$), on-chip thermal supervisory circuits abruptly trigger Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), downclocking accelerator frequencies by up to $60\%$. This doubles forward inference latency ($T_{\text{infer}}: 25\text{ ms} \to 70\text{ ms}$), blowing past the $50\text{ ms}$ action chunking deadline and tripping uncommanded emergency stops. Systems must maximize arithmetic intensity via INT8/FP8 quantization within on-chip SRAM and deploy **Proactive Thermal Cadence Scaling** ($H=16 \to 32$, $50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$ at $T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C}$) to stabilize thermals below the DVFS cliff.

#### Pitfall: False Sharing and Cache Line Ping-Pong in Lock-Free Ring Buffers {.unnumbered}
Allocating producer sequence counters (`head_sequence`) and consumer sequence counters (`tail_sequence`) on adjacent memory addresses within the same 64-byte hardware cache line in shared SRAM mailboxes bridging asymmetric processor cores. When the producer on Core 0 writes an updated `head_sequence`, the hardware cache coherency protocol invalidates the entire 64-byte cache line in Core 1's local cache. When the consumer on Core 1 subsequently reads `tail_sequence`, it incurs a cache miss and stalls its pipeline. Over high-frequency IPC streams ($1000\text{ Hz}$), this continuous **cache line ping-pong** creates severe bus contention, inflates synchronization latency from $<50\text{ ns}$ to hundreds of microseconds, and introduces non-deterministic timing jitter. Firmware must enforce strict cache line isolation using alignment specifiers (`alignas(64)`) on all independently modified shared variables.


## Chapter Summary and Forward Handoff to Chapter 11

This chapter established how cognitive workloads are deliberately placed across heterogeneous silicon fabrics. Physical AI rejects the cloud illusion of fungible compute, mapping multi-rate cognitive stages across Cloud, Host MPU, Neural Accelerator NPU, and Real-Time MCU based on cadence ($0.001\text{ Hz} \to 1000\text{ Hz}$), memory bandwidth, thermal dissipation, and physical trust boundaries.

The architectural discipline of heterogeneous compute placement rests on three core pillars:

1. **Non-Fungibility of Physical Silicon:** Time-critical safety loops ($1000\text{ Hz}$) cannot be offloaded across non-deterministic wireless networks (5G/Wi-Fi) or general-purpose operating system schedulers. Generative policies propose candidate trajectories under expiring **Intent Leases** ($\tau_{\text{lease}} \le 100\text{ ms}$), while bare-metal microcontrollers maintain exclusive hardware authority over motor inverters.
2. **Deterministic Interconnects and Zero-Copy IPC:** Shared Unified Memory Architectures (UMA) require hardware **AXI QoS Priority Arbitration** (`QoS=15` for MCU, `QoS=10` for NPU, `QoS=4` for Camera DMA) to prevent video streams from starving real-time control loops. Inter-processor communication must use lock-free SRAM ring buffers with strict 64-byte cache line isolation (`alignas(64)`) to eliminate mutex context switching and cache line ping-pong.
3. **Thermodynamic Co-Design & Arithmetic Intensity:** Moving bits across off-chip DRAM consumes $750\times$ more energy per byte than on-chip arithmetic ($150\text{ pJ}$ vs $0.2\text{ pJ}$). Quantizing trajectory models to reside permanently in on-chip SRAM ($I_{\text{arith}} \ge 120\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$) eliminates DRAM bus heating. Real-time proactive thermal cadence scaling dynamically adjusts chunk horizons ($H=16 \to 32$) and inference rates ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$) at $T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C}$, preventing catastrophic DVFS downclocking cliffs ($>85^\circ\text{C}$).

### Advancing to Chapter 11: Runtime Governance and Safety Systems

Having established where cognitive workloads reside across heterogeneous silicon in Chapter 10, we now advance to **Chapter 11 (Runtime Governance and Safety Systems: Hazard Mitigation, Dual-Heartbeat Watchdogs, and Governed Flywheels)**. 

In Chapter 11, we explore how distributed physical agents are governed during continuous operations:

- **Dual-Heartbeat Hardware Watchdogs:** Structuring bidirectional hardware and software heartbeats between Linux host MPUs and bare-metal MCUs to detect hung threads and trigger microsecond safety fallbacks.
- **Dynamic Hazard Escalation:** Implementing multi-tier fallback hierarchies (Category 2 trajectory hold $\to$ Category 1 controlled deceleration $\to$ Category 0 hardware Safe Torque Off) governed by runtime safety monitors.
- **Expiring Intent Lease Protocols:** Enforcing bounded execution leases that automatically safe the platform when semantic planners fail to refresh commands within their allocated latency budget.
- **Governed Data Flywheels:** Capturing real-world failure edge cases and out-of-distribution physical interactions for fleet-level retraining while preserving runtime determinism and operational safety.
